title: A framework for separating dephasing from decoherence in matter-wave Bell interferometers
authors: S. Kannan, Y. S. Athreya, X. T. Yan, S. S. Hodgman, A. G. Truscott
abstract: Matter-wave Bell interferometers provide a sensitive probe of mass-dependent decoherence in entangled quantum systems. The degree of entanglement is obtained from the Bell-correlation amplitude of this interferometer. For observing potential mass-dependent decoherence, a reliable interpretation of any observed reduction in the Bell correlation amplitude is required, which depends on three factors: geometric dephasing, environmental decoherence, and technical dilution from source and detection statistics. In this work, we present a framework based on the Schwinger SU(2) mapping to separate these contributions into local unitaries or dissipative channels. We show that by evaluating the Bell correlation at zero interferometer path difference, it is possible to extract a source-distribution-independent Bell correlation amplitude reduction. When this framework is extended to involve atoms of different mass, we show that the known differential decoherence channels are negligible at current sensitivity. This yields a concrete bound at which a dual-species Bell interferometer would begin to signal differential decoherence beyond the known systematics, opening the way for such systems to probe new physics, such as mass-dependent decoherence mechanisms.
summary: The paper develops a rigorous framework using SU(2) mapping to analyze matter-wave Bell interferometers, enabling the separation of geometric dephasing from true environmental decoherence. By analyzing measurements at zero path difference, the authors extract a source-independent measure of entanglement loss. This provides a concrete diagnostic tool for testing fundamental physics, such as mass-dependent decoherence mechanisms in quantum gases.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a robust theoretical framework to disentangle geometric dephasing, environmental decoherence, and technical measurement limitations when interpreting Bell correlations in matter-wave interferometers.
main_result: The authors present a method using the zero path difference (ZPD) condition that yields a source-distribution-independent extraction of the true Bell correlation amplitude reduction. They show this framework can set concrete null benchmarks for detecting mass-dependent decoherence in dual-species systems.
method: The analysis employs the Schwinger SU(2) mapping to model momentum-mode occupation states as pseudospin operators, allowing systematic separation of unitary (geometric) and dissipative (decoherence) noise channels.
model_or_system: The physical system is a matter-wave Bell interferometer, specifically utilizing Rarity-Tapster geometries with momentum-entangled atom pairs. The theory models the measurement process using spin-$ rac{1}{2}$ operators on a Bloch sphere.
key_observables: Bell correlation amplitude ($\langle A angle$), which quantifies entanglement; the coincidence fringe measured at zero path difference (ZPD).
important_parameters: Zero interferometer path difference ($\delta x = 0$); low-mode-occupancy limit ($ ar{n} \ll 1$); mass difference between species in dual-species tests.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a low-mode-occupancy regime and relies on the symmetry properties of the interferometer geometry (e.g., RT symmetry) to cancel certain systematic errors like linear magnetic gradients.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic setup of the Rarity-Tapster interferometer, the mapping from momentum modes to pseudospin states on a Bloch sphere, and how path asymmetry ($\delta x$) introduces measurable geometric phase shifts.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing the measurement formalism using SU(2) mapping, then deriving the dependence of the correlation function on path differences ($\delta x$), identifying ZPD as the key diagnostic point to eliminate geometric dephasing, and finally extending this framework to test for differential decoherence between atomic species.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, generalizable theoretical tool for interpreting high-precision quantum measurements in cold atom systems. By rigorously separating noise sources, it elevates the field's ability to distinguish fundamental physics signals from technical artifacts, which is crucial for next-generation quantum sensors.
